title: What India’s Protests Reveal About the Future of Liberalism
author: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
text: Podcast What India’s Protests Reveal About the Future of LiberalismA Conversation With Pratap Bhanu Mehta Published on October 22, 2026 Play Listen to the Episode 69 minutes 00:00 / 1:08:46 0.5×1×1.5×2× MP3 Close audio player Print Print this article Save Sign in and save to read later Close Share What India’s Protests Reveal About the Future of Liberalism A Conversation With Pratap Bhanu Mehta Share in email Share on Facebook Share on X Share on LinkedIn Article link: https://www.foreignaffairs.com/podcasts/what-indias-protests-reveal-about-future-liberalismhttps://www.foreignaffairs.com/podcasts/what-indias-protests-reveal-about-future-liberalism Request reprint permissions here.Episode Details Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is facing his biggest challenge since taking office in 2014. But in an essay in Foreign Affairs, Pratap Bhanu Mehta argues that the youth protests that have swept New Delhi don’t just pose a test for Modi’s authority—they may also mark an inflection point for India itself. “The future of Indian democracy,” Mehta writes, “hinges on whether this contest opens up more democratic space or leads to greater repression.”Deputy Editor Kanishk Tharoor spoke with Mehta, an analyst of Indian politics and University Lecturer at Princeton University, on October 19 about Modi’s power, about what these protests can and cannot achieve, and about what the battle in India means for the future of liberal democracy around the world.Sources:“A Democratic Reckoning in India” by Pratap Bhanu Mehta“The Everything Crisis” by Pratap Bhanu MehtaThis is a rough transcript of the conversation. Please consult the underlying audio prior to citation.Kanishk TharoorPratap, welcome back to The Foreign Affairs Interview.Pratap Bhanu MehtaIt’s a great privilege to be back. Thank you, Kanishk.Kanishk TharoorWe’re speaking today at a moment of extraordinary youth upheaval, notably in India and in France, but elsewhere too. Unlike in France and Albania, these youth protests in India have remained largely nonviolent and peaceful. In the past weeks, tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of Delhi, even in the face of a big government crackdown. You’ve described these demonstrations in a recent essay in Foreign Affairs as one of the more consequential sorts of political challenges that India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi has faced since he came to power in 2014. We’ll talk about the underlying motivations and the implications of these protests, but I wanted to get a sense first: you’re sitting in Delhi, you’ve seen the marches in person. What has surprised you about these protests, and do you think they’ll persist?Pratap Bhanu MehtaI think the most surprising thing has been this sheer inventiveness. Just to take one example, the government has denied them a protest site, and they have just converted lots of different sites in the city into protest sites. The protests seem to attract a loose amalgam of groups, which has turned out to be an advantage in this case. One group is detained; another group shows up somewhere else. But the most powerful thing I think about the protests has been their utter fearlessness. I mean, the student leaders, Neha Bora, Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka, Dipke, have been detained several times. As we speak, two of them are still in custody; under what law or provisions they’re not entirely clear. They’ve been detained several times, and they’ve been astonishingly fearless in their ability not just to criticize, but almost to mock power, which is very unprecedented. There’ve been lots of protests around specific policies against Mr. Modi over the last 10, 15 years, the farmers’ revolt, the [Citizenship Amendment Act] revolt, but there is a kind of youthful mocking critique here, which the government has found it very difficult to counter.The other thing that I think has been surprising, I think, and this has evolved over the course of the movement, as you know, the protest started in July over an exam leak, is the way in which they have been able to connect four different issues. So one was the issue of exam leaks, which the students were protesting against. Then it became a protest over the special intensive revision of the electoral rolls, which the Election Commission is conducting basically to ascertain who should be on the voting list and who should not be on the voting list, and there’s some fear that this process is leading to exclusion of significant numbers of voters. But they’ve been able to link these two specific issues to a much more general critique of authoritarianism, that they’ve kind of drawn the link between the two, that there is actually something about the authoritarianism of this government and evidenced in the fact that it does not even allow protests from students.They’ve actually tried to kind of convert all of this into a package. And that’s also, I think, actually quite remarkable because it has actually attacked some of the foundations of the regime rather than just specific policies.Kanishk TharoorIn the essay you wrote for us last week, which is titled [“A Democratic Reckoning in India”], you distill that two of the precipitating causes of not just the protests this past month, but also those in the summer, were elections and exams. You noted that elections and exams have played a very important role in the history of modern India in guaranteeing citizens a certain sense of equality and fairness, at least in their ostensible administration. I wonder, for those of our listeners who haven’t had the luxury of reading your essay, could you explain the roles that elections and exams play in India and why controversies around them have succeeded in inciting so much upset and unrest?Pratap Bhanu MehtaFor elections, the case is straightforward, right? It’s the one institution where all citizens feel free and equal. As you know, one of the remarkable things about Indian democracy is large numbers come out to vote. Turnout rates are higher than often Western democracies. The sense of agency: this one moment where the system recognizes you in a society that is otherwise extraordinarily unequal and disempowering. Exams, I think, have a kind of parallel function, which is most forms of social interaction involve hierarchies of status. Mostly, you get ahead by relationships of kinship, inherited social capital. Now, of course, we know inherited social capital also matters for things like preparations for exams, but there is still this idea that there’s something objective that the exam is assessing, which is not at the discretion of power. People can’t arbitrarily change the rules of the game. If you get 60 marks and I get 59, you of course are a better candidate than me. So the sense of objectivity and fairness that exams project have been extraordinarily important in an unequal society like India.It is also, for a vast majority of lower-middle-class, poor students, their only ticket to social mobility. They don’t have inherited capital, they don’t have inherited social capital, right? But if you do well at these tests, it could open up a ladder of opportunity in the civil services, in college admissions, in admissions to technology institutes, possibly even going abroad. On the other hand, given how scarce opportunities are in India, if you fail at these exams, it can be actually devastating and crushing. I mean, you can see the kind of ladder of opportunity almost being pulled away. So there is something very visceral and existential about our relationship to these exams. And elections and exams, between them, are the two places where the Indian state says, “We have a system that is, at least in principle, potentially fair and equal.”Kanishk TharoorLet’s dig into elections first. The controversy around them is a process that’s been enacted by the Election Commission called the Special Intensive Revision, which is a process in which authorities are going over India’s vast rolls of voter lists and flagging names that, for whatever reason, they think should not be there. And in this process, 130 million names have been flagged for potential removal. On its face, what is wrong with a process like this? One would think that it’s normal for a country to want to ensure the integrity of a list like that. What has been problematic about this bid to revise India’s voting lists?Pratap Bhanu MehtaSo you’re right. I mean, in principle, a Special Intensive Revision is entirely justified, and it’s the Election Commission’s constitutional duty to protect the integrity of the voting lists, right? But by that same duty, it also has an obligation to ensure that every voter who deserves to be included actually gets included. Now, this time, there were four basic changes in the way in which the process was carried out compared to 2002, which was the last time this was extensively carried out. I mean, there are interim revisions, but those are not as extensive.The first was the Election Commission changed the requirements for what kind of identity papers and proofs would count as adequate for being included in the voting list. So it increased the number of identity requirements. There used to be a presumption that if your name had been on a prior voting list—so let’s say you were on the 2002 voting list, or let’s say you were on the voting list in the 1990s—if you had been on the voting list in a prior election, your name would be included unless there was a specific reason to kind of exclude it. They did away with that presumption.The third thing they did, which was... So typically, the way the verification works is there are these local election officials, often school teachers actually deputed for this kind of duty, or local government officials, who basically go house to house verifying these electoral rolls. So they’ll come to your house, they’ll ask you for identity papers, they’ll check spellings, so on and so forth. And these election officials then basically certify whether you deserve to be included or not. And historically, that local certification has counted for a lot. This year, apparently what happened, or at least in this round of SIRs, is they introduced some kind of software, which was controlled by the central Election Commission in Delhi, which could use its own algorithm to send notices to electors that their names had come under question, even if local officials had actually verified it. So this raised the specter of perhaps more central control over voting lists.And the last and final and perhaps the most egregious thing, which particularly happened in the West Bengal election... So there was an election in West Bengal a few months ago, and the SIR process in the state of West Bengal was just started a few weeks before the election. Something like 2.7 million voters were put on the kind of disputed list. Now, normally what happens in a process like this is you can appeal your exclusion. Technically, somebody can also appeal your inclusion. Somebody can file a complaint saying, “We know so-and-so has been included. We have reason to think there shouldn’t be.”In this case, what was astonishing was that while their cases were under appeal, they decided to go ahead with the election, and the Supreme Court put its seal of approval on the idea that all those electors whose names were disputed would not be allowed to vote in this election. And the Supreme Court then blindly added, “If it turns out that they were eligible to vote, they can easily vote in the next election,” which is absolutely astonishing. So you’re actually not even given the full due process by your own rules, the chance to actually succeed and make sure that every elected official is included. And then as a result, I mean, lots of people were excluded, and that cumulatively raised suspicions of gross incompetence at the very least, if not outright mala fide in manipulation.And I think the final nail in the coffin in the story was a kind of series of investigative reports by newspapers, principally the Indian Express, although it has to be said in fairness that the opposition had been raising these issues for a while, particularly Rahul Gandhi, but these investigative reports came up with evidence that there was lot of dissension within the Election Commission about the processes that the Election Commission was adopting, but they went ahead anyway.So I think, cumulatively, it just adds to the suspicion that the Election Commission is failing in its constitutional duty to ensure every eligible voter gets to vote and potentially setting up processes that could be open to manipulation.Kanishk TharoorWhat you’re outlining here are concerns and suspicions about the integrity of two supposedly independent institutions, the Supreme Court and the Election Commission, which are supposed to be beyond the reach of governmental interference, right?Pratap Bhanu MehtaVery much so. Look, first of all, these protests are a result of the fact that the independent institutions failed in the first place. And the central demand of the protestors is the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Mr. Gyanesh Kumar. I mean, he’s kind of become a symbol for incompetence or potentially something worse. So the central animating demand centers around the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar. It centers around a full auditing of the SIR process, if not canceling of the SIR process. But as I said, it’s, I think, one of the first revolts in recent memory which you can attribute directly to the failure of independent institutions. So if the Supreme Court had said, “We will ensure that this process takes place in a manner that no person who’s eligible to be included will be excluded,” it could have provided the kind of oversight and the processes that actually would have, I think, assured most of the citizenry that their rights will be protected.There’s also kind of sidelight and proximate causes, which is one of the groups that is spearheading this protest is this incredibly named party, the Cockroach Janta Party, and the name Cockroach Janta Party came from a remark that the Chief Justice of India offhandedly made in a completely unrelated litigation, the litigation related to actually how senior counsel are designated in the Indian bar, where he seemed to, in a sense, imply that there were a lot of unemployed lawyers and stuff who were acting like cockroaches almost. But India’s young and unemployed, struggling, aspirational youth kind of adopted that term for themselves. They set up the social media handle and, within a week, got 22 million followers. This is, I think, the only moment I can think of. It is literally the Supreme Court by its abdication in the judicial side and then by creating a kind of structure of discourse where young people finally felt there were no avenues of redress left that actually instigates, or at least is the kind of proximate cause for this moment.Kanishk TharoorBeyond elections, the other sort of precipitating cause of a lot of these protests are exams, and I think exams tie into the larger problems bedeviling the Indian economy. Why are students up in arms about the way exams have been administered?Pratap Bhanu MehtaSo the answer is very simple, which is there’ve been a series of exams where papers have been leaked in advance to some students, giving them unfair advantages. Now, this has happened a lot in the past in India. I mean, it’s a frequent occurrence. There’s so many exams. The stakes are so high that the incentives to cheat, to distort the system, are also very high. But I think what’s distinctive about this time is, one, it’s happening repeatedly; it’s happened to a series of exams, but it’s also the fact that Mr. Modi’s government actually centralized the conduct of exams in a new national testing agency. So more and more exams are being entrusted to this national testing agency. And in part, the centralization of the process has also made the central government and the prime minister, and the central education minister a direct focal point. So the movement was successful in getting the resignation of India’s education minister, Mr. Dharmendra Pradhan, because the central government was held to be directly responsible for these leaks and distortions in the exam process.Kanishk TharoorYour former colleague Yamini Aiyar has written on a few occasions in Foreign Affairs about India’s jobs crisis. Millions of people enter the workforce every year, but there aren’t enough jobs, enough good-paying jobs as well, to soak them up. And Aiyar, she sees the inability of the economy to produce those jobs as evidence of India’s sort of uneven transition from socialism to capitalism, its sort of inability to deregulate certain sectors and shed its commitments to forms of statism. How do you see this larger problem? It seems a lot bigger than the surface-level contest between political parties.Pratap Bhanu MehtaAbsolutely. I mean, not surprisingly, I actually agree with much of Yamini Aiyar’s kind of analysis. And I think in the backdrop is a kind of larger problem about the transition of the Indian economy from a low-productivity economy to a high-productivity economy that generates enough jobs for its young people. But I think there’s something very specific about this revolt, which I think also one has to bear in mind, which is the challenges of the economy, in a sense, have been around for the last 20, 30 years. India has clocked impressive growth rates, and those growth rates are real. I don’t want to cast doubt on those growth rates. I mean, the headline number is seven percent, in a sense, for this year. But the growth has a particular character, which is it seems to have benefited the top ten percent. It seems to have allowed the state enough resources to create a kind of welfare coalition for the bottom 25, 30 percent, and the growth in India’s welfare state has been quite impressive.But there’s a kind of large chunk of the middle, which is actually trying to move to high productivity and high-wage jobs that is actually not finding that transition easy. By all estimates, graduate unemployment is roughly in the range of 23 to 25 percent. But what is even more distinctive about this revolt, if you look at the kind of social composition of this revolt, is there’s a lot of lower-middle-class students, but a lot of students whose parents were the greatest beneficiaries of liberalization—perhaps people of my generation in some senses, who benefited from the opportunities of liberalization—and their children are actually struggling to think of a trajectory where opportunities for them would be as easy as it was for their parents, at least of a certain strata. The remarkable thing about this movement, which is very rare in India, is that actually a lot of middle-class kids are part of this protest. And behind that is a kind of anxiety of almost a downward mobility for a certain class, in addition to the general problems that we have of not expanding opportunities as quickly as we shouldKanishk TharoorYou’ve observed that the Cockroach protests were successful in unseating the education minister. Do you think it’s possible that the protest will do the same in toppling the chief election commissioner, which seems to be the main demand? And if that does happen, would that mollify the protesters and then maybe sap their energy, and we’ll see fewer people out on the streets?Pratap Bhanu MehtaSo there’s one big success the protest already has, and I think it is worth underlining, because it’ll probably get lost in the kind of debate over the protest, which is they have already forced the Election Commission to modify their procedures on the special intensive revisions. So the Election Commission has made a commitment to go out and reach out to voters whose name has been excluded. They’ve simplified the procedure. In places like Delhi, a lot of names that were excluded are suddenly being included. So in some senses, they’ve already produced a form of accountability, I think, which is actually quite remarkable because…I think forcing the resignation of the chief election commissioner is going to be very difficult for this movement. It’s going to be very difficult for this movement because accepting that he’s responsible would actually implicitly call into question the legitimacy of the kind of election process. And I think, in that sense, the stakes are higher. It’s not just questioning a policy disagreement or a lapse in a particular administration of policy. I think it would be a kind of admission that there might have been something kind of illegitimate about the process. I think the second reason why I think forcing a resignation in this case will be difficult is I think the government is beginning to sense, and this lay behind the kind of crackdown of the protests, the move by the central government to bring out the police and paramilitary forces in large numbers to prevent the protest from happening, that if they’re successful in eliciting the election commissioner’s resignation, this could set off a chain reaction of emboldening the opposition on issue after issue. But more importantly, it also sets up the potential for defections within government.One of the ways in which the government ensures loyalty of its own cabinet ministers, its own officials, is this kind of assurance that you’re accountable to nobody else but us. So whatever directives you implement, whatever actions you take, the only yardstick by which you will be held accountable is the yardstick the government gives. But if this process gets institutionalized, as it should be in a democracy, that you will be constantly accountable to the opposition; you’ll be constantly accountable to civil society. It could potentially, in a sense, weaken Mr. Modi’s ability to keep control over his own government. I mean, officials might begin to say, “Look, we can’t follow this directive. Tomorrow, somebody’s going to ask tough questions of us.” He also loses one of his most important instruments by which he’s maintained this absolutely kind of iron grip on power, which is, in a sense, the loyalty of his own government.Kanishk TharoorSo then what you’re sketching is something of an impasse. What do you think happens next?Pratap Bhanu MehtaAt the moment, I think the logic seems to be the government seems to be hoping that some of the sting of the SIR controversy will lessen simply because more and more electors might actually get included. So when the final voting lists are published, if the number of excluded people is much smaller than what we are anticipating now, that that actually takes the sting of the protest. So that’s on the carrot side. On the stick side, frankly, I think the government is going to double down on its authoritarianism. There’s already evidence of that. As I said, they’ve been repeatedly arresting students, extending their judicial custody without, in a sense, any reason. They’re trying to create a discursive structure suggesting that all of this is being funded by foreign forces, these are kind of anti-nationals. I think the government’s playbook in the past has been to kind of divide and rule, to use coercion, and I think you’ll see that playbook come out in kind of full force. And they’re hoping between these two measures, it just, in a sense, the protest, in some ways, fizzles out.The next big test of the government’s legitimacy is going to be an election in India’s largest state, in Uttar Pradesh, sometime early next year. And I think that the government is hoping if they can win that state election, their legitimacy will have been restored, and people will forget about this like they forgot about the farmers’ protest.Kanishk TharoorThe principal opposition party, the Congress Party under Rahul Gandhi, has sought to position itself as a kind of champion of these protests. Even as you’ve noted, they’re primarily driven by sort of young people, Gen Z and so forth. What do you make of that kind of positioning? And do you see here an opportunity for this opposition, which has frankly been quite disoriented in the last 12 years, not able to really mount a significant challenge at least in elections at the national level to Modi’s grip on power? Do you see an opportunity here for it to up its game?Pratap Bhanu MehtaIt’s definitely an opportunity. I think you’re already seeing evidence for it. One of the paradoxes of this protest is that the issues that the students are raising, particularly around the SIR, Rahul Gandhi has been trying to raise for almost a year and was getting relatively little traction, and I think part of it was just this general skepticism that opposition leaders oppose for opposing’s sake. I think what the students did and what the various news reports around dissensions with the Election Commission did, the students don’t carry much baggage. The government doesn’t have a set playbook against them in the way that it has had against the Congress Party. So if the Congress Party accuses the government of authoritarianism, the government simply reminds it that it imposed the emergency almost 50 years ago, right? So what the students did was they disrupted the government’s playbook, first of all. And I think, in that sense, the Congress was shooed to stand behind the students rather than stand in front of them.I think the second thing it has done is it has finally given the opposition an issue, which is... The opposition has been trying to make this argument that democracy is in danger for a long time, and it has had no electoral traction. But I think the SIR issue gave them something tangible and concrete around which to unite. So practically, every single opposition party has at least now signed on to the skepticism of the SIR process.Third, what it has done, and I think this is a new kind of version of Congress we are seeing, is that Rahul Gandhi is leading street politics himself. So they themselves have been at the barricades. I mean, you must have seen all those kinds of films of Rahul Gandhi trying to climb up the barricades, Priyanka Gandhi being arrested, being detained, put on a bus, and so forth. At least it has given a signal to a lot of people that there is a little bit of determination to actually, in a sense, buckle up for a street fight, if need be, because one of the questions hovering over the Congress Party has always been kind of the commitment of its leaders.I mean, there’s always been this kind of strange commitment deficit the Congress Party’s been associated with the last 10 years. Even people who agree with it say it just hasn’t had the kind of energy, the street smarts, the street fight. And I think it has given the Congress an opportunity to show that it is made of a little bit sterner stuff than we thought it is, but it’s still got a long way to go. I think what the opposition will have to demonstrate is not just that they can come around processions and rallies once every five or six months, but they can actually effectively work as a cohesive political unit at the level of political tactics, at the level of strategizing about elections, at the level of projecting a coalition that is actually capable of governing, not just critiquing.Kanishk TharoorI’ve had the privilege of working with you over a number of years now, and I do remember on previous occasions around protests, or even two years ago when the Congress Party and the opposition did reasonably well in elections and really ate into Modi’s majority, that you have found in these events causes to think that Modi’s sort of unquestioned authority was under threat, that there was a sort of more democratic challenge rising to his growing authoritarianism. In the coming months and years, how will we know that this moment is different, that these protests have had a sort of different effect on Indian politics and society than previous eruptions have had?Pratap Bhanu MehtaI think there are three possible yardsticks you could use. So the first yardstick is, do they actually produce change? And as I said, I think one of the remarkable things about the Cockroach Party is that it’s already produced change. It’s for the first time got a minister in the Modi government to resign. It has got the Election Commission to at least respond, even if it’s officially not acknowledging its mistakes. I mean, the idea that we could actually hold the government accountable for its actions, that had become such a strange idea in the last few years that I think it has certainly lessened that sense of impunity. So I think if you go by those yardsticks, I think it’s different.I think the second yardstick is, to be honest, we don’t know how much nationwide support this protest has. There’s a lot of sympathy for the students, but will it actually translate into a kind of electoral rejection of Mr. Modi? We are still a long way off from that. But the fact that the government itself fears these protests so much, and there’s a bunch of 20-year-old kids who had no organization, basically had a social media handle, and the government says, “We have to bring out the most unprecedented deployment of police and paramilitary forces in Delhi,” almost 40,000, “to prevent this protest from happening,” it takes away the designated site to protest, suggests to me that they themselves fear something. So even if you don’t see the kind of big surge of crowds which they’ve prevented from assembling... I mean, just to give a little anecdote, 245 trains into Delhi were canceled the day of the protest so that people couldn’t come. 47 metro rail stations were shut down so that people couldn’t come. So the government is already acknowledging the power of the movement independently of its size.And as I said, I think what you are seeing is you’re seeing a lot more people speaking up. I mean, even the investigative journalism that the Indian Express carried out, one of the questions for the Indian media is: why were these kinds of stories not possible in the last 10 years? This kind of knockdown story, which really just left no room for ambiguity that the Election Commission was at least being incompetent, if not mala fide. I think that’s on the kind of plus side.But I also fear, as I suggested, that the government will have to rely on more outright coercion to govern and establish its authority. And as you know, both things are possible together, which is that you have more resistance. But that more resistance actually converts what would have otherwise been authoritative acts into merely acts of power, and so you rely more and more on suppression, rule, bylaw, the course of the state to actually exercise political control. I think you’ll see both of these kinds of processes in motion together.Kanishk TharoorI want to switch gears a little and zoom out. The last time you were on this podcast, I asked you about this notion, which I think is still common, that the rise of Modi at his dominance has proved that India’s supposed liberalism was mostly aspirational, that it was only a sort of thin elite veneer over what is fundamentally a deeply illiberal country. You rejected that idea completely. You noted that India’s secular liberal founders had huge popular support and that the politics of Hindu nationalism and many other sorts of conservative populist projects are quite modern, not ancient. And in some respects, and we see this in the US too, this is a contest over a kind of cultural authenticity, what really represents a society. Do these protests, as you’re seeing them, do they participate in that contest in any way?Pratap Bhanu MehtaOh, I think they do participate in that contest. I think they do participate in the contest in the sense that these protests at least hold out the possibility of renewal of three very core dimensions of liberalism. One is, of course, that citizens are free and equal. I know it’s a bare minimum for liberalism. But the electoral process and the fairness of the electoral process is not merely procedural. As I said, it is the embodiment of one of the kind of central moral tenets of liberalism, and the fact that actually you have a movement trying to defend that is not nothing. I don’t think it’s merely protest. I think it actually does speak to the moral core of liberalism.I think the second thing I think it does speak to the moral code of liberalism, which is, in part, what kind of society does liberalism envision? Liberal freedoms, a kind of lightness of being, where you don’t live in fear. You don’t live in fear of being arrested by the state on arbitrary grounds. You don’t live in the fear of authoritarianism. I think one of the things that these protests are trying to do, I think most importantly at the level of moral psychology in the liberal self, is to say that the core of liberalism is to be able to breathe that air where you are free from fear of arbitrary state power. So I think it is trying to reclaim that space. Whether it’ll be successful or not, that’s a subject for long discussion, but I think it is, in some senses, trying to claim that space.And I think the third thing in the Indian context, which is I think important, is so much of Indian politics in the last few years has been centered around divisive issues of religion, Hindu nationalism, often of caste. Here is a movement that’s saying, “One of our principal aims is to hold the government accountable for education.” Those kinds of moments have been actually relatively rare in Indian politics. So again, I think one should not overestimate their prospects of success. There’s a long struggle ahead for these movements. But I think the way in which they have framed what they’re trying to do, reading the preamble of the Constitution, the leaders kind of wear T-shirts with Gandhi and Ambedkar. I do genuinely think they are trying to fight for a kind of democratic renewal.Kanishk TharoorIn our new issue, the November/December issue of Foreign Affairs, you have a wonderful essay on the seeming global crisis in liberalism. It’s called “The Everything Crisis.” I should note that when we use the word liberalism in this conversation, we’re referring to the political philosophy. We’re not using it as it’s often used in the United States to denote sort of left or center ideas. In this essay, you write about two books by avowed liberals, one by the Nobel winning economist, Daron Acemoglu, and the other by the journalist Adrian Wooldridge, and both these books are sort of part of the literature of alarm that sees, say, the 2016 Brexit vote and the election of Donald Trump in the same year and all the turmoil in Western countries since then that sees all of that as part of a wider breakdown. I think India often fits into this narrative too because Modi came to power sort of roughly at the same time in 2014.You are seeing this conversation about liberalism and its discontents both from within the West and from outside it. Do you see strong parallels between, say, the Indian experience of the past decade and the American one?Pratap Bhanu MehtaActually, I think there are striking parallels, I mean, although these two countries are as far apart in terms of where they are in terms of their economic development, in terms of their history, in terms of their geographical location. The parallels I see, I think, are as follows. The first, most obvious one, and I think which many of these books touch on, I think Daron Acemoglu is particularly good in it, which is that liberalism is not just a set of political institutions—democracy, limited government, checks and balances, opportunities for people to exercise political agency, and practiced public justification. Part of what sustains liberalism is a kind of social contract that the government that the system produces will be able to produce a widely shared prosperity.And part of Daron Acemoglu’s argument, the argument of many liberals, many others actually, is that the crisis of liberalism is first and foremost a crisis of the performance of liberal government, that somehow the promise of shared prosperity, even though the headline growth numbers look good in both countries, I mean 2.5 percent for the United States, an economy its size is staggering, seven percent for India is staggering, yet underlying it is a sense of immense inequality, the growing power of oligarchy, and I think this anxiety in a sense around the middle class, whether in a sense the future will be better than in some senses as the past. And by the way, this is not just an anxiety in India or the United States. I mean, one of the points I kind of try and make often is this crisis, this challenge, also afflicts authoritarian systems, like China, which is if you look at the share of labor in the kind of prosperity that has been generated in the last 20, 30 years, it’s not that China looks spectacularly better than the United States.So there is something about the social contract in the global kind of moment that we are in where all societies are dissatisfied with the performance of their governments. They’re simply not producing the kind of shared prosperity. Now, the diagnosis may differ. Some think it’s due to exogenous technological change; some think it’s due to globalization, but I think the waning confidence in liberal governments about that—I think that’s one, I think common background condition. I think the second common thing, which I think is remarkable in both countries, a similarity, is a kind of tension between two dimensions of democracy. Most of us as liberals think of the core of democracy as checks and balances, restrictions on arbitrary government power, separation of powers, those kinds of institutions in some senses that make for the rule of law.But I think in both countries, you’ve had leaders and forces, populist leaders, Donald Trump, Narendra Modi, who have actually convinced significant sections of the electorate that part of the reason why we were not getting effective government was precisely those liberal institutions that were meant to check and balance power, and the argument is in part that these institutions got captured by elites. These institutions gave so many veto points to different actors that you actually cannot express the will of the people to come together to do something jointly. And that, in a sense, then underwrites the claim to even stronger executive power. Now, it has to be set as an aside that the argument for strong executive power has also come from the left. It has also, in different forms, come from the center. But I think in its purest distillation, the idea that government should be concentrated in executive power, the executive becomes the embodiment of the people against all kinds of elites that use these institutions, including, by the way, the professions, the universities, the media, to thwart the genuine will of the people.And the third, and I think final commonality is that what gives this executive power legitimacy is not just that it promises to cut through the clutter of democracy as it were, the checks and balances, the messy compromises of democracy, but it also justifies itself in the name of nationalism. This leader is the stand-in for the project of making the nation great, making India great, making America great. The executive serves as a kind of embodiment of that national greatness. And the test of your legitimacy is not whether the Supreme Court approves of you. It’s not whether you uphold basic constitutional rights. The test of the legitimacy of government is does the state manage to further the national identity and civilization aims of that society, make America great, a certain conception of American history and American memory. And I think there’s a parallel project in India in a sense with Hindutva.Kanishk TharoorAnd there’s a parallel project, I suppose, in China as well where there’s been an attempt, under Xi Jinping, to recover the inheritance of Chinese civilization, and in Russia too, an appeal to the past as well. In your essay, you make this really fascinating argument that the crisis of liberalism is not really just a crisis of liberalism. It’s many of the dysfunctions that seem to be afflicting liberal democracies are also shared by all sorts of other countries. What do we learn when we find parallel problems among liberal and illiberal countries?Pratap Bhanu MehtaI think a couple of things. I mean, this is obviously a pretty complicated argument and a little speculative in some ways. But if you take modernity, let’s roughly say from the kind of 18th century onwards, post-French Revolution, even a country like China is, in some senses, an heir to that revolutionary tradition, there’s been this kind of persistent tension, which is on the one hand, modernity promises freedom and emancipation. Even many illiberal projects have, in principle, been committed to that as an end state at some point. Once we kind of get rid of all the sources of oppression, some kind of emancipation and freedom will be possible where we are completely the author of our own destinies. We literally make and remake ourselves. There’s a really kind of enchantment, in a sense. I think we’re in modernity about freedom, and it unleashes that desire—freedom against authority, freedom against arbitrary power.On the other hand, modernity also unleashes a range of institutions, bureaucracies, capitalism, nation-states, which seem to belie the promise that we can make and remake the collective institutions, in a sense, according to our collective will. They seem to thwart our freedom in different ways. To use Max Weber’s kind of famous phrase, we often seem to inhabit this kind of iron cage of modernity. It’s a tension that has been at the heart of modernity since the 18th century. Almost every modern theorist of modernity grapples with one or other form of this tension. And to that extent, whether it’s socialist societies, whether it’s capitalist societies, whether it’s liberal democracies, all of them have had to kind of face some kind of tension of this kind between the aspiration to self-determination that modernity unleashes and the reality of us being embedded in institutions that we seem to be able to do very little to shape or reshape, particularly the nation-state form, particularly capitalism, particularly modern forms of juridification and bureaucratization of social life.Sometimes we manage to shape them enough, push back enough; democracy can push back against them enough, to give people a sense of agency. But when they experience them, the collective world as not being a world of shared prosperity, as being run by oligarchies, we come back right into the sense that there is something deeply constraining about modernity as well. And I think it’s this persistent tension between the institutions of productivity, efficiency, organization that modernity requires, and the quest for freedom and self-determination that it unleashes. That seems to be like a universal condition almost that nobody seems to have quite come to fully terms with.Kanishk TharoorA few years ago on another podcast, you made the interesting claim that the triumphant ideologies of the 20th century are not, as often suggested, liberal democracy and capitalism, but rather two other ones, nationalism and feminism. And on nationalism first, I’m struck by the number of liberals in recent years, and I’m thinking, for example, of Francis Fukuyama, but there are many others, but liberals who have become keen to stress the virtues of liberal nationalism, to reclaim patriotism, and I think distance themselves from the stereotype of the liberal as some kind of flighty, jet-setting, cosmopolitan. What do you make of that project of trying to reconcile national belonging and universal liberal values?Pratap Bhanu MehtaThere are, I think, two distinctions that are important in this debate. So one, when we contrast liberal nationalism, what is the opposite of liberal nationalism? And typically the opposite of liberal nationalism is ethnic nationalism, some kind of ethnonationalism where your citizenship is defined by some inherited particular trait. And in terms of that contrast, liberal nationalism works. It seems to be more universal. The color of your skin, your religion, your social identity does not, in a sense, determine the possibility of you becoming a member of a society. It’s really determined, in a sense, by your fidelity and allegiance to a kind of constitutional framework.But there is a challenge, I think, even liberal nationalism has always had to face, which is liberalism just doesn’t have a theory of membership. So even if you wanted a liberal national society, let’s say the United States, think of it as a kind of quintessential liberal nationalist project, think of the modern Indian Constitution in its purest form as a liberal nationalist project, you still have to ask this tricky question: who gets to be in and who gets to be out? And liberals basically have had to fudge an answer on that question. The question comes in the case of politics very clearly on the issue of immigration. What is a proper liberal theory of immigration? One simple answer is that a liberal society is a voluntarily constituted community of faith, and it has the right to keep people out of that community.But that doesn’t still solve the criteria, what is a correct liberal response to immigration? Some liberals say, “Well, let’s allow the immigration of the talented, not in a sense low-cost labor immigration.” It’s actually not clear why that is a liberal response. I mean, it may be a practically appealing response to democratic publics. One of, I think, the challenges for liberalism is that it has always struggled with the issue of membership. And frankly, the best it can do is pragmatically fudge this issue, hoping that enough people buy into the policies it recommends.But there’s a second thing, I think, which is very important in 2026 about liberal nationalism. My view is liberal nationalism never went away, even in the era of the end of history, globalization, 1989 to 2009. I think it’s a little bit of a mistake to think of it as an era where globalization and cosmopolitanism was supplanting liberal nationalism. I think it’s a mistake to think that, in part, because one of the reasons countries signed on to globalization—the United States signed on to globalization—was because it thought globalization could be an instrument of national power. It was a more intelligent way of preserving national prosperity in some ways, particularly after the crisis of the 1970s and 1980s. The way you keep inflation down is you arbitrage on low-labor costs in the world, for example, or something like that. Globalization was not a kind of cosmopolitan alternative to liberal nationalism. It was one means of realizing its prospects.But the attractiveness of globalization was around one proposition where it did not see national competition in a zero-sum game. Underlying it was this kind of perhaps Panglossian hope that there is a way of countries creating structures of interdependence where they can both further in their national goals, they can become more prosperous, they can promise their citizens better future, and yet they don’t have to be locked into a zero-sum competition with other nations. I think in 2026, the question for liberal nationalism is not, do you oppose external nationalism? That’s actually an easy argument in some ways. The immigration argument, as I said, has always been a difficult argument and will remain one for liberalism. I think the more difficult argument is, where does liberal nationalism stand on this question of the zero-sum character of global politics? Is the competition between China and the United States a competition where nation-states say, “Somebody’s got to win this competition, and in a sense establish their primacy”?Outside the United States, there’s a lot of skepticism about liberal nationalism in the sense that the skepticism says, “Look, within the US, people begin to say, “Well, liberal nationalism is a way of discovering social solidarity.’ From outside the United States, people think, “You know what is this liberal nationalism really about? It is about the fact that the rest of the world began to actually catch up, China actually began to catch up, global intra-country inequalities actually began to decline, and it is the fear or the anxiety that generated around America’s primacy in some ways and a primacy that, by the way, both administrations, Republican and Democrats, have explicitly said they’re committed to preserving.”Now, what that has done is that has actually made global politics much more of a zero-sum game. And if global politics becomes a zero-sum game, it is probably not going to be able to sustain liberal values in the long run. I think that is the question I think we have to honestly ask every liberal nationalist, which is, do you think liberal nationalism is... We can understand the social functions it performs domestically, the sense of identification it produces, but do you envisage a world order which is a race for primacy between independent, sovereign, even liberal national states? And if it is a race for primacy, what happens to global public goods? What happens to managing global public risks? And what happens to this vision that liberalism always had that actually all of humanity, in some senses, could actually simultaneously be better off without it being a kind of zero-sum competition?Kanishk TharoorWe’re drifting into a conversation about the so-called liberal international order, which I wasn’t expecting, actually. But let me ask you, Mark Carney, the prime minister of Canada, made quite an impact earlier this year with his speech at Davos, where he talked about the end of this order and suggested that middle powers—and I think of which he included his country, but I imagine many would also include India—would have to chart a way forward without the United States. When you are thinking about liberalism, writ large and its fate at a sort of global level, say, in the absence of an active, strong United States interested in advancing liberalism, what kind of order would be best and most conducive to liberalism?Pratap Bhanu MehtaAs you know, Kanishk, institutionally and sociologically, one of the things that sustains liberal societies is a kind of balance of power, a distribution of power, internally as well. Whenever power becomes too concentrated, it is often a threat to liberalism. I think it was Gentili who said, “The existence of great power by itself is a provocation,” should be a provocation particularly to liberals. I think the challenge at this moment, and I think this is the context of Mark Carney’s kind of call to arms, is that you have two of the most powerful countries in the world that, from the point of view of the rest of the world, have actually gone rogue in different ways, maybe not to the same extent. They’ve gone rogue in the sense that neither of them is committed to building structures of global cooperation and international institutions that can sustain an open, fair, and just global order.The United States certainly is engaged in reckless wars that have had extraordinary impact on the rest of the world. Arguably, even a lot of the kind of crisis you see in Europe at the moment can be directly attributed to some of the consequences of this war, completely unmindful of the humanitarian and collateral damage these wars are doing. These are two countries that are also intent on weaponizing their economic progress. The United States has imposed economic sanctions in several countries. China has just introduced export controls. These are the two countries that control most of the world’s advanced technologies, particularly AI. In fact, arguably, these are the only two countries in the game.Now, imagine if you’re in the rest of the world and you say the two powerful, most powerful forces, countries in the world have no commitment, serious commitment, to global public goods, have no serious commitment to global justice... and moreover, even that, we could live with. I mean, the international order has never been just. It has always been hierarchical, but they’re actually committed to weaponizing every bit of power they have for their own national interest. What will the alternative for the rest of the world will be? It’ll have to be to create some kind of counterforce to the two superpowers. So it’s not an anti-American coalition; it’s not an anti-China coalition. It’s a coalition that is basically saying, “How do we ensure that the risks of these two superpowers weaponizing their power are actually mitigated?” So the rest of the world is now looking to sign trade deals with each other. They’re looking for supply chain resilience.Now, the brute fact of the matter is that the rest of the world at the moment just does not simply have the power to be able to effectively check and balance two superpowers. I mean, that is just the kind of the reality of global power in some senses at the moment. But I think it certainly wants to try and build up the kinds of institutional architecture that is potentially an inoculation against both of these poor superpowers. I mean, 10 years ago, the discussion in Asia was, which power are you hedging against? Are you hedging against China, or are you hedging against the United States? Now, the discussion is we need to hedge against both.Kanishk TharoorAmong your other victors of the 20th century, you’ve included feminism. And I wanted to ask you about that because, in the United States and many other countries, you have at the moment sort of very strong anti-feminist politics in charge, and you have prominent cultural forces pushing for the return to family values and the centrality of the household and seeking to return women to roles of reproduction and caring. At the same time, here in the US, Gen Z is the first generation in which the majority of women identify as feminists. How do you see this dual, this sort of contest of emancipatory cultural energies? I suppose I’m thinking not just of feminism, but of the sort of bundle of ideas and platforms that gets termed identity politics or wokeness. How do you see the contest between that and of the political reaction to it? How do you see it playing out in the coming years?Pratap Bhanu MehtaThis is a wonderful question and a difficult one. I think one way to think about this is to separate out three different components in a sense of the kind of identity politics story. One, I think, the simple aspiration of identity politics historically has not been anti-universalistic. In fact, it has been the claim that, historically, societies were marked by structures of inequality—race, caste, all kinds of other kinship structures, gender—and that if you’re to truly build a society of free and equal individuals, you sometimes have to take these structural inherited inequalities into account, self-consciously into account, so that you can dismantle them. But the purpose of dismantling them is not to install new hierarchies of identity. The purpose of dismantling them is to, in a sense, emancipate individuals from the oppressive weight of these social hierarchies. So there’s a form of identity politics that has historically been not just compatible with liberal politics, but in some senses a kind of extension of liberal politics.There’s a second kind of aspiration, I think, in almost all modern identity politics movements, which goes back to this idea of radical self-determination that modernity unleashes, that there’s a kind of romance around modernity, which is we can author our own lives, we can make of ourselves whatever we wish. Part of what we want to make of ourselves also extends to even naming what our identity is. Why should I be trapped by the tyranny of labels that inherited social structures put on us, and specifically when they came with how opportunities were structured? So there’s this incredible quest for kind of self-definition that modernity unleashes, and I think that quest for self definition is kind of inevitable in modernity. It’s going to be kind of difficult to, I think, turn the genie back even in very oppressive societies. The pushback against encrusted categories of gender, the idea of making and remaking yourself through fashion, consumerism, all kinds of ways, pushes back against. There are two forms of identity politics that you might say are a natural outgrowth of the desire for individual freedom.I think there was a third aspect added to it over the last 15, 20 years, which is what, in part, people were revolting against. This was a kind of more controversial, almost epistemological claim: that reason can be collapsed into identity, that what makes particular forms of reasoning valid is determined by who is actually giving those reasons, in some sense. So from the plausible premise that your social context can actually determine the validity of arguments, that social power can actually shape forms of reasoning people are allowed to make. From that plausible premise, some people drew the conclusion that reason just is, in a sense, power all the way down. There is no such thing as shared public justification. And I think there’s been a kind of revolt against that proposition. I actually don’t think many people sincerely believe that proposition, but yes, there is a lot of politics that in a sense speaks that language. In some senses, that identity is reason in some ways.And then there’s the final, I think, twist, which goes to the heart of contemporary politics: that in this unleashing of freedom, of course, a lot of traditional social structures were completely shattered. The family has been re-imagined beyond belief in the last 30, 40 years. The place of children in society, the value of children in society, some would argue regrettably, has been radically reimagined in some senses. And these forms of emancipation, of course, have also been threatening to many social groups, including men, who were beneficiaries of older hierarchies. And in part, there’s a kind of longing in some quarters to recreate those social hierarchies, which I don’t think is going to be possible. I think that genie is, in some senses, out. I mean, I think to that extent, I think modernity is, in some senses, kind of irreversible. But it manifests itself as a politics of resentment precisely because, with a straight face, you cannot actually say, “Let’s reinstitutionalize patriarchy.” I mean, it’s just a very, very difficult argument. Some people are trying, but it is actually a very, in some senses, difficult argument to make.Now, the challenge for, I think, our societies is, and their conservatives may have a point, that there are particular social forms, like the family, for example, although they’ve changed over time, that have given people a sense of meaning, social and moral identity, anchored their social mores. And the worry is, if you dismantle those, will we be able to artificially create new social forms that can perform exactly those functions or similar functions that those old social forms did of nurturing children, of creating stable identities, of privileging commitment as a form of human relationships so that not every human relationship is just transactional? I think the liberal optimism is: yes, new forms of institutional life will emerge. I think the conservative pessimism is that what you will get is a kind of radical atomization of society. Freedom will shade over into a kind of complete narcissism of a certain kind, which is what often the old generation accuses the young of. And that, in a sense, will lead to a kind of fragmentation of society of the kind we have not seen.Kanishk TharoorWell, Pratap, you’ve taken us from the streets to the realm of ideas, and we’ll look forward to pursuing many of these arguments and more in our pages and elsewhere.
